title: have to and must
subtitle: I have to go / I must go
summary: Use have to and must to say that something is necessary, and know when have to is the only choice and why mustn't and don't have to mean different things.

lesson.heading: have to = it is necessary
lesson.text: **I have to do something** = it is necessary to do it, I am obliged to do it. Have to has all the usual tenses: have to / has to, had to, have had to.

examples.text: You can't turn right here. You **have to turn** left.
I **have to wear** glasses for reading.
Robert can't come out with us this evening. He **has to work** late.
Last week Tina broke her arm and **had to go** to hospital.
I **haven't had to go** to the doctor for ages.

lesson.heading: Questions, negatives and the future
lesson.text: We use **do/does/did** in questions and negative sentences (for the present and past simple). For the future you can say **I'll have to ...**, **I'm going to have to ...**, **I might have to ...** or **I may have to ...**.

examples.text: What **do** I **have to do** to get a new driving licence?
'**Did** you **have to wait** a long time for a bus?' 'No, only ten minutes.'
They can't repair my computer, so I**'ll have to buy** a new one. or ... I**'m going to have to buy** a new one.
We **might have to change** our plans. or We **may have to change** ...
examples.note: = it's possible that we will have to change them

left.label: must / have to = your own opinion
left.text: You can use must or have to when you give your own opinion - to say what you think is necessary, or to recommend something.
examples: It's later than I thought. I **must go**. or I **have to go**.
I haven't spoken to Sue for ages. I **must phone** her. / I **have to phone** her. (= I say this is necessary)
Mark is a really nice person. You **must meet** him. / You **have to meet** him. (= I recommend this)

right.label: have to = a fact
right.text: We use have to (not usually must) to say what someone is obliged to do. This is a fact, not the speaker's own opinion.
examples: I **have to work** from 8.30 to 5.30 every day. (a fact, not an opinion)
Jane **has to travel** a lot for her work.

lesson.heading: must in rules; had to for the past
lesson.text: We use **must** in written rules and instructions. But we use **had to** (not must) to talk about the past.

examples.text: Applications for the job **must be received** by 18 May.
I went to the meeting yesterday, but I **had to leave** early.

left.label: mustn't = don't do it
left.text: You mustn't do something = it is necessary that you do not do it.
examples: You must keep this a secret. You **mustn't tell** anyone. (= don't tell anyone)
I promised I would be on time. I **mustn't be** late. (= I must be on time)

right.label: don't have to = you don't need to
right.text: You don't have to do something = it is not necessary to do it (but you can if you want).
examples: You **don't have to come** with me. I can go alone.
I **don't have to be** at the meeting, but I'm going anyway.

lesson.heading: have got to
lesson.text: You can use **have got to** instead of have to. The meaning is the same.

examples.text: I**'ve got to work** tomorrow. or I have to work tomorrow.
When **has** Helen **got to go**? or When does Helen have to go?

lesson.text: Must has no past form and no do/does/did questions: for the past say had to, and for questions and negatives use do you have to / I don't have to.

exercises.prompt: Joe starts work at 5 am every day, which means ___ at four.
exercises.explanation: A present fact about what Joe is obliged to do: he has to get up.

exercises.prompt: We nearly missed the bus this morning. ___ to catch it.
exercises.explanation: This morning is past, so we use had to.

exercises.prompt: Ask about the age you need to be for a driving licence. Put the words in order.
exercises.answer: How old do you have to be to have a driving licence?
exercises.explanation: Questions with have to use do/does: How old do you have to be?

exercises.prompt: Was the exhibition free, or ___ to go in?
exercises.explanation: A past question needs did: did you have to pay?

exercises.prompt: You can let me know later what you want to do. You ___ now.
exercises.explanation: It is not necessary to decide now: don't have to decide.

exercises.prompt: A man was slightly injured in the accident, but he ___ to hospital.
exercises.explanation: Past and negative: didn't have to go (= it was not necessary).

exercises.prompt: When Patrick starts his new job next month, he ___ 50 miles to work every day.
exercises.explanation: Future obligation: will have to (or is going to have to). Must has no future form with will.

exercises.statement: I couldn't get a taxi last night. I must walk home.
exercises.explanation: I couldn't get a taxi last night. I had to walk home. We use had to (not must) for the past.

exercises.statement: You must come and see us again soon.
exercises.explanation: Correct. The speaker gives their own opinion / recommendation, so must is fine (You have to come is also correct).

exercises.statement: Tom isn't going out this evening. He must study for his exam.
exercises.explanation: He has to study for his exam. This is a fact about what Tom is obliged to do, not the speaker's opinion, so have to is more natural.

exercises.prompt: What ___ to get a new driving licence?
exercises.explanation: Questions with have to are formed with do/does: What do I have to do?

exercises.prompt: Which phrase completes each sentence: mustn't or don't/doesn't have to?
categories: don't have to / doesn't have to

items.text: There's a lift in the building, so we ___ climb the stairs.
I promised Kate I'd call her tomorrow. I ___ forget.
Sophie likes weekends because she ___ get up early.
You ___ be a good player to enjoy a game of tennis.
You should keep trying to find a job. You ___ give up.
I ___ eat too much. I'm supposed to be on a diet.
We have plenty of time before our flight. We ___ check in yet.
